chapters.name: Chapter 1: The front of the house

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Restaurant jobs and the path up
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Match entry-level restaurant jobs to their duties and the credentials that help you get them.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of restaurant jobs, you will match each entry-level job to its main duties and the first credential or training that helps you get it, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
A restaurant has two sides. The front of the house (FOH) is where guests are: the host greets and seats them, the busser clears and resets tables, the server takes orders and brings food, the food runner carries plates, and the bartender makes drinks. The back of the house (BOH) is the kitchen: the dishwasher keeps dishes and tools clean, the prep cook cuts and portions food before service, and the line cook cooks orders during service.
Many people start as a dishwasher, busser or host and move up: dishwasher to prep cook to line cook to sous chef; busser or host to server to shift lead to manager. Showing up on time and learning every station is how you move up.
Credentials help. Many states or counties require a food handler card; a course such as ServSafe Food Handler from the National Restaurant Association is one common way to train for it. Servers who pour alcohol may need state alcohol server training such as ServSafe Alcohol. High school students can join ProStart, a two-year culinary and restaurant management program. Later, cooks can earn American Culinary Federation (ACF) certifications such as Certified Fundamentals Cook. The Restaurant Ready program, run with community groups, trains people not connected to school or work.
This course prepares you; it does not give you any card or certificate. Always check what your state, county and employer require.
Words to know:
- Front of the house (FOH): the part of a restaurant where guests are: host stand, dining room, bar.
- Back of the house (BOH): the kitchen, dish area and storage.
- Food handler card: a card showing you finished approved food safety training; required in some states and counties.
- ProStart: a two-year high school program in culinary arts and restaurant management.
- ACF: the American Culinary Federation, which certifies cooks and chefs in the United States.
Official sources:
- National Restaurant Association: ServSafe Alcohol and ServSafe Food Handler
- National Restaurant Association Educational Foundation: ProStart
- National Restaurant Association Educational Foundation: Restaurant Ready
- American Culinary Federation: certification
Try it now: Fold a paper in half. Write FOH on one side and BOH on the other. List every job from this lesson on the right side with one duty each. Circle the job you would like to start in and write the credential that would help you get it.
You can now name the jobs in the front and back of a restaurant, say what each does, and name a credential that helps you get hired.

check.q: Which job is in the back of the house?
check.why: The prep cook works in the kitchen; the others work where the guests are.

check.q: You want to serve drinks with alcohol. Which training might your state require?
options: Alcohol server training such as ServSafe Alcohol
check.why: Many states have alcohol server training rules; check your state's page.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Taking an order the right way
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Take a table's order, ask about allergies and repeat the order back.
This lesson builds toward: Given a table of guests in a role play, you will take an order in the right order of service, ask about allergies and repeat the order back, with no missing items or changes.
Most mistakes happen when an order is taken. A server who follows the same steps every time makes fewer mistakes and earns better tips.
Greet the table within a minute or two, say your name, and offer drinks. When they are ready, ask: "Does anyone have a food allergy I should know about?" Write the order by seat number, so the runner knows who gets which plate. Write every change, such as no onions or dressing on the side.
Repeat the order back to the table before you leave. Then enter it in the point-of-sale system (POS) or write the ticket clearly. If a guest has an allergy, mark it on the ticket and tell the kitchen or manager in person too. Never guess whether a dish is safe; ask the kitchen. If a guest has trouble breathing or a bad reaction, call 911 (or your local emergency number) and get the manager.
Check back a few minutes after the food arrives, clear plates when everyone is done, and bring the check when the table asks or is clearly finished.
Step by step:
- Greet the table, say your name and offer drinks.
- Ask about food allergies.
- Write the order by seat number, with every change.
- Repeat the order back.
- Enter it in the POS or write a clear ticket; mark any allergy and tell the kitchen in person.
- Check back after the food arrives; clear and bring the check.
Words to know:
- Steps of service: the order of tasks a server follows for every table.
- Seat number: a number for each chair, so the right plate goes to the right guest.
- POS: point-of-sale system: the screen where orders are entered and paid.
- Ticket: the printed or on-screen order the kitchen cooks from.
- Modifier: a change to a dish, like no onions or extra sauce.
Try it now: Role play with a friend or family member (or play both parts out loud). Take an order for three people from any menu, by seat number, with at least one change and one allergy. Repeat it back. Then check your paper: is every item and change there?
You can now take an order step by step, ask about allergies, write it by seat number and repeat it back.

check.q: Why write an order by seat number?
options: So the right plate goes to the right guest
Because the POS needs a phone number
So you can skip repeating it back
check.why: Seat numbers let anyone carrying the food put each plate in front of the right person.

check.q: A guest says she is allergic to peanuts. What do you do?
options: Tell her the food is probably fine
Write it down and hope the cook sees it
Pick a dish for her yourself
Mark it on the ticket and tell the kitchen in person
check.why: An allergy is marked and said out loud to the kitchen; you never guess whether a dish is safe.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Your pay: hourly wage, tips and the tip credit
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check that a week of tipped pay meets the federal minimum and that tips were handled legally.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sample week of hours and tips, you will check that tipped pay meets the federal minimum and that no manager took a share of tips, using the federal rules and naming where to check your state's rule.
Under federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act), an employer may pay a tipped employee a cash wage as low as $2.13 an hour and count tips toward the rest of the $7.25 federal minimum wage. This is called the tip credit. A tipped employee is someone who regularly gets more than $30 a month in tips.
The rule: your cash wage plus your tips must reach at least $7.25 for every hour you work in the week. If they do not, your employer must pay the difference. Many states set a higher minimum wage, and some, such as California, Minnesota and Washington, require the full state minimum wage before tips. Check your state on the US Department of Labor's tipped wage page.
Your tips are yours. An employer may not keep any part of them. A tip pool, where tips are shared among workers, is allowed, but managers and supervisors may not take tips from the pool.
The IRS says to keep a daily record of your tips and to report cash tips of $20 or more in a month to your employer by the 10th of the next month. Tips are taxed income, so reporting them protects you.
Step by step:
- Add up the hours you worked this week.
- Multiply hours by $7.25 (or your state's minimum, if higher).
- Add your cash wage and your tips for the week.
- If the total is less than the minimum, the employer owes the difference.
- Check your state's rule on the US Department of Labor tipped wage page.
Words to know:
- Tip credit: the part of the minimum wage an employer may cover with tips (federal: up to $5.12 an hour).
- Cash wage: the hourly pay your employer pays you directly, before tips.
- Tip pool: a system where tips are put together and shared among workers.
- FLSA: the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law on minimum wage, overtime and child labor.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 15, Tipped Employees under the FLSA
- US Department of Labor: Minimum wages for tipped employees by state
- IRS: Tip recordkeeping and reporting
Try it now: Practice only, with made-up numbers. Sam worked 20 hours, was paid a $2.13 cash wage and got $70 in tips. Work it out: 20 x $7.25 = $145. Cash wage 20 x $2.13 = $42.60. $42.60 + $70 = $112.60. Is that enough? How much does the employer owe? (Answer: $32.40.) Then look up your own state on the Department of Labor tipped wage page and write its rule.
You can now check that a week of tipped pay reaches the minimum wage, spot an illegal tip practice, and keep a record of your tips.

check.q: Under federal law, what must a tipped worker's cash wage plus tips reach for each hour?
check.why: Cash wage plus tips must reach the $7.25 federal minimum, or the employer pays the difference.

check.q: Your manager takes a share of the tip pool every night. What is true?
options: Only on weekends is it legal
Managers and supervisors may not take tips from a tip pool
It is legal if the manager also busses tables
check.why: The FLSA bars managers and supervisors from receiving tips from a tip pool.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Kitchen basics and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Kitchen safety: knives, heat, floors and teen rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name common kitchen hazards and the safe action for each.
This lesson builds toward: Given a kitchen scene with a hazard, you will name the hazard and the safe action for knives, hot surfaces, wet floors, heavy lifts or equipment a teen may not use, for every hazard in the scene.
OSHA's young worker restaurant guide lists the main kitchen dangers: cuts from knives and machines, burns from fryers, grills and hot liquids, slips and falls on wet floors, strains from heavy lifting, and electrical hazards. Your employer must give you a safe workplace and train you.
Knives: use a sharp knife on a cutting board with a damp towel under it so it does not slide. Curl the fingers of your guide hand. Never try to catch a falling knife. Carry it point down at your side and say "knife" or "sharp" as you walk. Never leave a knife in a sink of water. Burns: say "hot" or "hot behind" when carrying anything hot, use dry towels or mitts (a wet towel lets heat through), and keep pan handles turned in. Floors: wear closed, slip-resistant shoes and clean up spills right away or put out a wet floor sign. Lifting: bend your knees, keep the load close, and ask for help with heavy boxes.
Teens: federal child labor rules limit kitchen work. At 14 and 15 you may not bake, cook over an open flame, use most fryers (only ones that raise and lower the baskets by themselves), or use power-driven slicers, grinders, processors or mixers. At 16 and 17 you still may not use, clean or set up meat slicers, meat grinders or commercial mixers. 14 and 15 year olds also have limits on hours. Your state may have stricter rules.
Knife skills, fryer use and equipment are learned in person from a trained cook or instructor. If you are hurt or see a danger, tell your manager right away.
Step by step:
- Look for the hazard: blade, heat, water on the floor, heavy load, machine.
- Use the safe habit: guard hand, dry towel, call out, clean the spill, lift with your legs.
- If you are under 18, check if the task or machine is allowed for your age.
- Tell a manager about any danger or injury.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency for workplace safety.
- Guide hand: the hand that holds the food while the other hand cuts; fingertips curled in.
- Slip-resistant shoes: closed work shoes with soles that grip wet or greasy floors.
- Child labor rules: laws on which jobs and hours are allowed for workers under 18.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Young Worker Safety in Restaurants eTool
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 2A, Child labor rules for restaurants
- US Department of Labor: YouthRules
Try it now: Draw a simple kitchen on paper: a stove, a fryer, a cutting board, a sink and a walk-in cooler. Mark three hazards with an X (for example a spill near the fryer, a knife in the sink, a pan handle sticking out). Next to each X, write the safe action. Then write which tasks a 15-year-old could not do in your drawing.
You can now spot kitchen hazards, use the safe habit for each, and say which kitchen tasks are off-limits for teens.

check.q: A knife slips off the counter. What do you do?
options: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and pick it up when it has landed.

check.q: A 15-year-old is asked to slice meat on a power slicer. What is true?
options: It is fine with gloves on
Federal rules do not allow it for a 15-year-old
It is fine if a friend watches
check.why: Federal child labor rules bar 14 and 15 year olds (and 16 and 17 year olds) from using power-driven meat slicers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Station setup, tickets and kitchen calls
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a station from a prep list and call out tickets and moves clearly.
This lesson builds toward: Given a prep list and a set of tickets, you will set up a station with mise en place and call out tickets and kitchen moves clearly, with every item ready before service and no missed calls.
Mise en place (say "meez on plahs") is French for "everything in its place". Before service, a cook reads the prep list, gets every ingredient, tool and container ready, and sets them up in the same spot every day, so nothing is missing when the rush starts.
During service, orders come in as tickets, printed or on a kitchen display screen. The expediter (expo) or chef calls each ticket out. You answer "heard" or "yes, chef" so they know you got it. Cook the oldest tickets first, and tell the chef right away if you are running out of something; when an item is gone, it is "86".
Kitchens are tight and busy, so people call out their moves: "behind" when you walk behind someone, "corner" when you turn a blind corner, "hot" or "sharp" when carrying something dangerous. Clean as you go: wipe your board, put tools back and keep your station neat.
Step by step:
- Read the prep list for your station.
- Gather every ingredient, tool and container on the list.
- Set them up in the same place every time; label and date containers.
- Check the list again before service: nothing missing.
- During service: answer "heard" to each call, cook the oldest tickets first, call out your moves, clean as you go.
Words to know:
- Mise en place: French for everything in its place: all ingredients and tools ready before cooking.
- Prep list: the list of what must be cut, portioned or made before service.
- Expo (expediter): the person who calls tickets and checks each plate before it goes out.
- Heard: what a cook says to show they heard a call.
- 86: kitchen word for an item that has run out.
Try it now: Pick a simple dish you can make at home, like a sandwich or a salad. Write a prep list for making it for 10 people. Then set up your mise en place on a table: every ingredient and tool you need in its place before you start. Write one thing you would have forgotten without the list.
You can now set up a station with mise en place, answer and work tickets in order, and call out your moves in a busy kitchen.

check.q: What does mise en place mean?
options: Everything in its place, ready before service
check.why: Mise en place means every ingredient and tool is set up before cooking starts.

check.q: You walk behind a cook carrying a hot pan. What do you say?
check.why: Calling "hot behind" warns the cook so they do not step back into you.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting hired: your restaurant job plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a 30-day plan to get your first restaurant job.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own goals and schedule, you will write a 30-day restaurant job plan with a target job, a credential, availability and a pitch, with a date and an official link for each step. Given a list of restaurant jobs, you will match each entry-level job to its main duties and the first credential or training that helps you get it, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Restaurants often hire fast, sometimes the same week. Many ask you to apply online or in person and may invite you to a short interview or a working interview (a stage, said "stahzh"), where you work part of a shift so they can see you. Ask whether a working interview is paid; under federal law, time you spend doing productive work for the business is usually work time that must be paid.
Managers care most about three things: when you can work, whether you show up on time, and whether you are friendly and willing to learn. Weekends, nights and holidays are the busiest times, so being open then helps. Apply in person between meal rushes (for example mid-afternoon), not during lunch or dinner.
If you have a record, many restaurants hire people with records. Be honest when asked, keep it short, and talk about what you have done since, such as training, work and your food handler card. Programs like Restaurant Ready and local reentry and workforce centers can connect you with employers.
Your plan pulls it all together: the job you want, the credential you will get first, your availability, a checklist of the shift, and a 30-second pitch.
Step by step:
- Pick a starting job and two real places to apply.
- Pick one credential to get first (for example a food handler card) and find its official page.
- Write your weekly availability.
- Write a shift checklist for the job: setup, during the shift, closing.
- Write a 30-second pitch: who you are, when you can work, why you will be reliable.
- Put a date on each step in the next 30 days.
Words to know:
- Working interview (stage): a short trial shift so the restaurant can see you work.
- Availability: the days and hours you can work each week.
- Pitch: a short spoken introduction that says why someone should hire you.
- Fair-chance employer: an employer willing to hire people with criminal records.
Official sources:
- National Restaurant Association Educational Foundation: Restaurant Ready
- US Department of Labor: YouthRules (work permits and hours for teens)
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 15, Tipped Employees under the FLSA
Try it now: Final task: make your Restaurant Job Plan on one page. Write the job you want and two real places to apply, the credential you will get first and its official page, your weekly availability, a shift checklist (setup, during, closing), and a 30-second pitch. Put a date on each step in the next 30 days. Read the pitch out loud twice.
You can now write a 30-day plan to get a restaurant job and give a short pitch to a hiring manager.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Job and places to apply No clear job, or no real places named. Names one starting job with its main duties and two real places to apply. Also names the next job up and what it takes to get there. Credential with official page No credential, or a link that is not official. Names one credential (for example a food handler card) and its official state, county or program page. Also notes whether the job needs alcohol server training or, for a teen, any state work permit. Shift checklist Missing setup, during-shift or closing tasks. Lists setup, during-shift and closing tasks for the job, including mise en place or table setup. Adds the call-outs and allergy steps the job uses. Safety and pay No safety habits or pay check in the plan. Lists two safety habits for the job and how to check tipped pay or hourly pay against the minimum. For a teen, names tasks the learner may not do at their age; for a tipped job, names the state rule. Pitch and dates No pitch, or no dates on the steps. A 30-second pitch with availability and reliability, and a date on each step in the next 30 days. The pitch was practiced out loud with another person and improved. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: When is a good time to walk in and apply at a restaurant?
options: In the middle of the lunch rush
Between meal rushes, such as mid-afternoon
check.why: Managers have time to talk between rushes, not when guests are waiting.

options: "I can work any time, I guess."
"I'm Jordan. I can work nights and weekends, I have my food handler card, and I'm always on time."
check.why: It says who you are, your availability, a credential and why you will be reliable.
